questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A seed plant bears ovules exposed on cone scales and does not enclose its mature seeds in a fruit. Which group fits both observations?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Gymnosperms.
Why: An exposed ovule can mature into a naked seed. Gymnosperms bear seeds without the enclosing ovary that later becomes a fruit; the two observations therefore reinforce the same identification. The ovule is borne directly on a cone scale rather than inside a carpel. Because no ovary wall develops around it, the mature seed is not enclosed by a fruit.
Why not the others: (B) Angiosperm ovules are inside an ovary and their seeds are enclosed in fruit. (C) Bryophytes reproduce by spores rather than seeds. (D) Pteridophytes also lack seeds and produce spores.
Key point: Locate the ovule before fertilisation and the seed after it.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: In a flower, sepals, petals and stamens appear above an ovary to which the floral tube is fused. Which pair describes it?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Inferior ovary; epigynous.
Why: Fusion of the floral tube around the ovary puts the apparent insertion of the other whorls above it. That relative position defines an inferior ovary and an epigynous flower, regardless of the flower's size. Use the level at which all other whorls arise relative to the ovary, not the flower's orientation on the page. The fused floral tube surrounds the ovary and makes it inferior.
Why not the others: (A) Hypogynous whorls arise below a superior ovary. (C) A perigynous cup surrounds but does not fuse to a superior ovary in this way. (D) Combines incompatible relative positions.
Key point: Judge ovary position from the insertion and fusion of floral parts.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The figure compares three cell fractions after independent repeat isolation. Which fraction most strongly supports a peroxisome identification, using both positive and negative markers?
options: A) Fraction P, because chlorophyll is abundant
B) Fraction Q, because ribosomal RNA is abundant
C) Fraction R, because catalase is enriched while chlorophyll and ribosomal RNA are low
D) All three equally, because each contains protein
questions.image_alt: Bar chart: P has high chlorophyll and low catalase; Q has high ribosomal RNA and low catalase; R has high catalase and low chlorophyll and ribosomal RNA; repeated preparations show the same pattern.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Fraction R.
Why: The figure shows strong catalase enrichment specifically in R, with little chlorophyll or ribosomal RNA. Catalase supports a peroxisome-rich preparation, while the low negative markers argue against chloroplast or ribosome contamination. Repeated isolation reduces the chance of a single separation accident. Catalase is a marker for peroxisomes because these organelles detoxify peroxide generated by oxidative metabolism. The other two marker profiles exclude a chloroplast- or ribosome-rich fraction even if isolation is imperfect.
Why not the others: (A) P's chlorophyll instead points to plastid material. (B) Q's RNA points to ribosome-rich material. (D) Protein occurs in many compartments and cannot identify an organelle.
Key point: Combine a positive marker with contamination controls.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The figure plots net photosynthesis against light at two fixed CO₂ concentrations and constant temperature. Which conclusion is best supported over the measured range?
options: A) Extra light always lowers net photosynthesis
B) High CO₂ prevents any light response
C) The two curves show that temperature changed
D) The low-CO₂ curve plateaus sooner, while high CO₂ permits a larger response to light
questions.image_alt: Net photosynthetic rate versus light intensity: the low-CO₂ curve rises then plateaus near 3 units; the high-CO₂ curve rises to about 9 units at higher light, at constant temperature.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Low CO₂ limits the light response sooner.
Why: At high light, the low-CO₂ trace is nearly flat while the high-CO₂ trace continues rising. Increasing light therefore adds little when carbon supply is limiting, but increases carbon fixation when CO₂ is less restrictive. The comparison holds temperature fixed. The two curves share the same light input; their separation therefore diagnoses the changed carbon supply. At low light both traces may be light-limited, so a CO₂ response emerges chiefly after irradiance is sufficient.
Why not the others: (A) Neither curve decreases over the shown interval. (B) The high-CO₂ curve responds strongly to light. (C) Temperature was controlled, so the difference cannot be assigned to it.
Key point: Interpret paired interventions rather than naming a limiting factor from one curve.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: At rest, heart rate is 60 min⁻¹ and stroke volume is 80 mL. During exercise, heart rate becomes 100 min⁻¹ while cardiac output rises by 25%. What is the new stroke volume?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 60 mL.
Given: Rest: heart rate 60 min⁻¹, stroke volume 80 mL. Exercise: heart rate 100 min⁻¹, cardiac output 25% higher.
Formula/Principle: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.
Step 1: Resting output = 60 × 80 = 4800 mL/min.
Step 2: Exercise output = 1.25 × 4800 = 6000 mL/min.
Step 3: New stroke volume = 6000 ÷ 100 = 60 mL per beat.
Why: Output is the product of two factors. Here the rate rises by 67% (60 to 100) but the output rises by only 25%, so the volume pumped per beat must fall. The question fixes the output, so the stroke volume has to be calculated from it, not assumed.
Why not the others: (B) 80 mL keeps the stroke volume unchanged, which would give 100 × 80 = 8000 mL/min, a 67% rise in output. (C) 100 mL copies the new heart-rate number and would give 10 000 mL/min. (D) 120 mL would give 12 000 mL/min, which is 2.5 times the resting output.
Key point: Work out the output first, then solve for the factor that changed.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A species has 2n=12. One homologous pair fails to separate in meiosis I of a male meiocyte; meiosis II is normal. Each of the four sperm is considered for fertilisation with a normal egg. Which zygote chromosome counts can result?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 11 and 13.
Given: 2n = 12, so a normal gamete has n = 6. One homologous pair fails to separate in meiosis I; meiosis II is normal.
Formula/Principle: Meiosis I separates homologues; meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
Step 1: After the faulty meiosis I, one daughter cell has 7 chromosomes (both homologues of the pair) and the other has 5 (neither).
Step 2: A normal meiosis II copies these counts into the sperm: two sperm with 7 and two with 5.
Step 3: A normal egg adds 6: zygotes have 7 + 6 = 13 or 5 + 6 = 11 chromosomes.
Why: The mistake happens in the first division, before any gamete is formed, so both daughter cells are already wrong. Meiosis II only separates sister chromatids and cannot restore the missing or extra homologue. So none of the four sperm from this meiocyte has the normal count.
Why not the others: (A) 12 needs a normal sperm with 6 chromosomes, and this meiocyte makes none. (C) 10 and 14 would need sperm with 4 or 8 chromosomes, which requires two pairs to fail, not one. (D) 12 and 13 describes nondisjunction in meiosis II of one daughter cell, where the other daughter still gives normal sperm; here the error is in meiosis I.
Key point: A meiosis-I error affects all four products; a meiosis-II error affects two.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Crossing two pure lines produces F₁ petals with distinct red and white patches; assays detect both parental pigment types. Which inheritance pattern best fits the observations?
options: B) Incomplete dominance producing a new pink pigment
C) Codominance of the two pigment traits
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Codominance.
Why: Both parental traits are visibly represented in the same F₁ rather than one masking the other. Detecting both pigment types supports simultaneous expression, not an intermediate pigment. Patchy expression is not an intermediate blended colour: the parental pigments remain distinguishable in different regions. The biochemical detection of both products supports simultaneous allele expression rather than dominance of one.
Why not the others: (A) Would hide white expression. (B) Predicts an intermediate blended phenotype rather than separate patches. (D) Nothing about the cross associates the trait with sex.
Key point: Distinguish coexistence of parental phenotypes from an intermediate one.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Equal doses of one antigen are given 40 days apart. Antibody rises slowly after the first dose but rapidly and much more after the second. Which mechanism explains the change without assuming a higher second dose?
options: A) The second injection bypasses antigen recognition
B) All innate immune cells become antigen-specific antibodies
C) The antigen becomes a different molecule after 40 days
D) Memory lymphocytes formed after first exposure respond faster on re-exposure
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Immunological memory.
Why: Initial exposure activates antigen-specific lymphocytes and leaves memory cells after the first response contracts. Those cells are already selected for the same antigen, so the second exposure has a shorter lag and larger response at equal dose. The first exposure creates selected lymphocyte clones and a memory pool. On re-exposure those clones expand and differentiate sooner, explaining the shorter lag and higher titre without requiring a larger antigen dose.
Why not the others: (A) Antigen recognition is still necessary. (B) Innate cells do not themselves turn into antibodies. (C) The experiment holds antigen identity fixed.
Key point: Compare response timing under a controlled repeat exposure.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A vector and insert are cut with the same restriction enzyme to produce complementary overhangs. A second vector has blunt ends. All ends have the groups required by ligase. What advantage is specific to the first vector–insert pair?
options: A) Complementary overhangs can anneal and align ends before covalent ligation
B) Ligase acts only on overhangs and never on blunt ends
C) Complementary ends ensure a single insert orientation in every case
D) Cutting makes both DNA fragments single-stranded throughout
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Alignment by base pairing.
Why: Complementary short overhangs transiently anneal, increasing the chance that the vector and insert ends remain together for ligase to seal the backbone. This is a pairing advantage, not an absolute chemical requirement of ligase. Compatible sticky ends increase encounter specificity through base pairing but do not create a covalent phosphodiester backbone. DNA ligase seals the sugar–phosphate nicks, making a stable recombinant molecule.
Why not the others: (B) Blunt ends can also be ligated. (C) Identical compatible ends can permit either orientation. (D) Only the overhang region is single-stranded.
Key point: Separate cohesive-end annealing from phosphodiester bond formation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: At equal intervals, a closed population is counted as 50, 90, 140, 180, 200 and 205; food supply is fixed and counts are accurate. Which interpretation fits the changing increments?
options: A) Exponential growth at a fixed per-capita rate
B) Growth slows as limiting resources become important
C) The population must have declined between every count
D) Immigration alone explains the final plateau
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Resource-limited growth.
Why: Increments rise at first but fall sharply near the last counts, even though the population remains positive and growing. With fixed food and no migration, density-dependent limitation is a coherent explanation for approaching a carrying level. The counts alone do not establish its exact value. As population size approaches environmental carrying capacity, per-capita resource availability falls and net growth slows. A rising total count can coexist with shrinking increments, so absolute increase alone does not prove exponential growth.
Why not the others: (A) Fixed exponential growth would not flatten this way. (C) Every recorded count rises. (D) Migration was excluded.
Key point: Compare successive increments, not just population sizes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Sex-linked recessive inheritance traced through an affected grandfather
questions.question: A woman's maternal grandfather had an X-linked recessive disorder. Her mother, her father and her husband are all unaffected. Assume complete penetrance and no new mutation. What is the probability that the couple's first child is an affected son?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1/8.
Given: Maternal grandfather affected (XᵃY). The woman's mother, father and husband are unaffected.
Formula/Principle: A father passes his only X chromosome to every daughter. A carrier mother passes Xᵃ to each child with probability 1/2. A son gets his X from his mother.
Step 1: The woman's mother received Xᵃ from the affected grandfather, so she is certainly a carrier (XᴬXᵃ).
Step 2: The woman received Xᴬ from her unaffected father and either X from her mother: P(woman is a carrier) = 1/2.
Step 3: P(child is a son) = 1/2.
Step 4: P(a son of a carrier receives Xᵃ) = 1/2.
Step 5: P(first child is an affected son) = 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.
Why: The allele is followed down the female line. An affected man's daughters are all carriers, so the woman's mother is a certain carrier even though she is unaffected. The woman herself has an even chance of having inherited it. Her husband is unaffected, so he cannot give the allele to a daughter in a way that makes her affected, and he gives a Y, not an X, to a son. So only a son can be affected, and only if the woman is a carrier and passes on Xᵃ.
Why not the others: (A) 1/4 leaves out one of the three halves; it is the chance that any given son is affected (1/2 × 1/2), not the chance that the child is a son and is affected. (B) 1/2 treats the woman as a certain carrier and the child as certainly a son. (D) 1/16 adds an extra factor of one half, as if the woman's mother were only a possible carrier.
Key point: Affected father → all daughters are carriers; carrier mother → half her sons are affected.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An mRNA coding region reads AUG | GAA | UCC | GCU | UAA. A single U is inserted immediately before the first base of the second codon, with translation still starting at AUG. What follows without consulting a codon chart?
options: A) Only one amino acid can change
B) Codon boundaries after AUG shift and several downstream amino acids may change
C) The start codon must disappear
D) Every codon after insertion remains unchanged
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Downstream frame shift.
Why: The ribosome reads consecutive, non-overlapping groups of three bases from the same initiation point. Adding one base after AUG changes which bases form every subsequent triplet until translation stops; even the location of a stop codon can change. An insertion not divisible by three changes every downstream codon boundary until a stop is encountered. Compare the new triplet grouping from the insertion point; simply adding one amino acid would assume the original frame remains intact.
Why not the others: (A) Assumes the insertion replaced only one whole codon. (C) AUG lies before the insertion. (D) Triplet grouping cannot remain the same after a one-base insertion.
Key point: Track reading positions, not just the inserted letter.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A freely filtered solute has plasma concentration 1 mg/mL and filtration rate 100 mL/min. Urine flows at 1 mL/min with solute concentration 10 mg/mL. With no tubular secretion, what fraction of the filtered solute is reabsorbed?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 90%.
Given: Plasma concentration 1 mg/mL; filtration rate 100 mL/min; urine flow 1 mL/min; urine concentration 10 mg/mL; no secretion.
Formula/Principle: Filtered load = plasma concentration × filtration rate. Excreted load = urine concentration × urine flow. Reabsorbed = filtered − excreted.
Step 1: Filtered load = 1 × 100 = 100 mg/min.
Step 2: Excreted load = 10 × 1 = 10 mg/min.
Step 3: Reabsorbed = 100 − 10 = 90 mg/min.
Step 4: Fraction reabsorbed = 90 ÷ 100 = 0.90 = 90%.
Why: A concentration alone says nothing about how much solute moves each minute, because the filtrate and the urine flow at very different rates. Both must be turned into amounts per minute. Since nothing is secreted, whatever was filtered but not excreted was reabsorbed.
Why not the others: (A) 1% is urine flow divided by filtration rate (1/100), which is the fraction of filtered water that is excreted, not solute. (B) 10% is the fraction of the filtered solute that is excreted. (C) 50% would need 50 mg/min in the urine, five times what is measured.
Key point: Compare loads (concentration × flow), not concentrations.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A drug prevents spindle microtubules from attaching to kinetochores but leaves DNA replication intact. Cells accumulate with condensed chromosomes and seldom separate chromatids. Which immediate process is blocked?
options: A) DNA replication in S phase
B) Nuclear envelope breakdown before spindle formation
C) Anaphase separation of sister chromatids
D) Cytoplasmic translation of spindle proteins
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Chromatid separation.
Why: Unattached kinetochores fail the spindle-attachment checkpoint, preventing the coordinated onset of anaphase. Chromosomes can condense, yet sisters cannot segregate reliably to opposite poles. DNA replication has already occurred under the stated condition. Kinetochores monitor bipolar attachment before anaphase. Although chromatids have already been copied, the checkpoint inhibits separation when spindle capture is incomplete, preventing unequal segregation.
Why not the others: (A) Is expressly unaffected. (B) Condensed mitotic cells have reached a later stage. (D) Protein synthesis is not the specified inhibited event.
Key point: An attachment checkpoint links spindle status to chromatid separation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two C₃ leaves are held at identical light, temperature and stomatal conductance. Leaf Q has higher O₂ and lower CO₂ around Rubisco than leaf P. What change is expected in Q?
options: A) More oxygenation and photorespiratory carbon loss
B) No change because Rubisco binds only CO₂
C) More net fixation because O₂ is the carbon source
D) Elimination of the Calvin cycle
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) More photorespiration.
Why: Rubisco can catalyse both carboxylation and oxygenation. Raising O₂ relative to CO₂ shifts competition toward oxygenation, initiating photorespiratory reactions that consume resources and reduce net carbon gain under the controlled conditions. It need not stop all carboxylation. Oxygen competes with carbon dioxide for Rubisco's active site. Oxygenation initiates photorespiration, consuming energy and releasing previously fixed carbon, thereby lowering net fixation despite equal stomatal conductance.
Why not the others: (B) Ignores Rubisco's oxygenase activity. (C) O₂ supplies no carbon for fixation. (D) Reduced net gain is not complete abolition of the cycle.
Key point: Compare competing substrates at the same enzyme.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Why is the H–N–H angle in NH₃ smaller than the H–C–H angle in CH₄?
options: A) Nitrogen forms four identical N–H bonds
B) Methane has a lone pair on carbon
C) Ammonia contains no tetrahedral electron-pair arrangement
D) A nitrogen lone pair repels bonding pairs more strongly than a bonding pair does
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Lone-pair–bond-pair repulsion.
Why: Both centres have four electron domains, but NH₃ has three bond pairs and a lone pair. The more spatially demanding lone pair compresses the angles between N–H bonds below the ideal tetrahedral angle of CH₄. A lone pair occupies more angular space around nitrogen than a shared bond pair, compressing the three N–H directions. Carbon's four equivalent bonding domains avoid this extra compression.
Why not the others: (A) NH₃ has three N–H bonds. (B) Carbon has four bonds and no lone pair here. (C) Electron-domain geometry is approximately tetrahedral even though molecular geometry is pyramidal.
Key point: Distinguish electron-domain and molecular geometry.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ionisation isomerism and the number of ions in solution
questions.question: The figure shows complexes P and Q, in which bromide and sulfate have exchanged places between the coordination sphere and the counter-ion position. What type of isomers are P and Q, and how many ions does one formula unit of each give in water?
options: A) Ionisation isomers; two ions each
B) Linkage isomers; two ions each
C) Ionisation isomers; three ions each
D) Coordination isomers; four ions each
questions.image_alt: Complex P is [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4, with sulfate outside brackets; Q is [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br, with bromide outside brackets.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Ionisation isomers; two ions each.
Why: P is \(\ce{[Co(NH3)5Br]SO4}\) and Q is \(\ce{[Co(NH3)5SO4]Br}\). They have the same composition, but the anion inside the coordination sphere and the anion outside it are exchanged, so they give different ions in solution. That is ionisation isomerism. Each formula unit breaks into one complex cation and one counter-ion: P gives \(\ce{[Co(NH3)5Br]^2+}\) and \(\ce{SO4^2-}\); Q gives \(\ce{[Co(NH3)5SO4]+}\) and \(\ce{Br-}\). Ligands inside the square bracket stay bonded to cobalt and are not released.
Why not the others: (B) Linkage isomers differ in which atom of the same ligand is bonded to the metal (for example –NO₂ and –ONO); here two different anions change places. (C) Three ions would need two counter-ions outside the bracket, but each complex has only one. (D) Coordination isomers need both a complex cation and a complex anion that exchange ligands, and neither salt gives four ions.
Key point: Ionisation isomers give different ions in solution; count only the ions outside the bracket plus the complex ion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Hydrogen ionisation from an excited level and photoelectron energy
questions.question: Hydrogen has Eₙ=−13.6/n² eV. A photon of energy 5.0 eV is absorbed by a hydrogen atom that is initially in the n=2 level, and the electron is ejected. What is the kinetic energy of the ejected electron?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1.6 eV.
Given: \(E_n=-13.6/n^2\ \mathrm{eV}\); the atom starts at \(n=2\); photon energy \(=5.0\ \mathrm{eV}\).
Formula/Principle: Energy needed to ionise from level n is \(0-E_n\). The electron's kinetic energy is the photon energy minus this ionisation energy.
Step 1: \(E_2=-13.6/4=-3.4\ \mathrm{eV}\).
Step 2: Ionisation energy from \(n=2\) is \(0-(-3.4)=3.4\ \mathrm{eV}\).
Step 3: Kinetic energy \(=5.0-3.4=1.6\ \mathrm{eV}\).
Worked derivation: \[\begin{aligned}E_2&=-\frac{13.6}{2^2}=-3.4\ \mathrm{eV}\\KE&=h\nu-(E_\infty-E_2)=5.0-3.4=1.6\ \mathrm{eV}\end{aligned}\]
Why: The electron is already in an excited level, so it is bound by only 3.4 eV, not by the ground-state value of 13.6 eV. A 5.0 eV photon therefore has more than enough energy to free it, and energy conservation gives the excess to the electron as kinetic energy.
Why not the others: (A) 3.4 eV is the ionisation energy from n = 2, not the energy left over. (C) 8.4 eV adds the binding energy to the photon energy (5.0 + 3.4) instead of subtracting it. (D) 5.2 eV subtracts the photon energy from the n = 1 to n = 2 excitation energy (10.2 − 5.0), which is not an ionisation balance.
Key point: Kinetic energy of the freed electron = photon energy − binding energy of the starting level.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A primary carbocation lies next to a carbon bearing a hydride and two alkyl groups. If a 1,2-hydride shift precedes nucleophile capture, what chiefly favours that shift?
options: A) It necessarily creates an aromatic ring
B) It converts the positive charge into a negative charge
C) It relocates positive charge to a more substituted, more stable carbocation centre
D) It breaks all carbon–carbon bonds
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A more stable carbocation.
Why: During a hydride shift, the C–H bonding pair migrates to the electron-deficient adjacent carbon. Positive charge then resides at the carbon that lost hydride, which is more substituted under the stated structure and stabilised by alkyl donation. The hydride moves with two bonding electrons; the formally positive site appears on the carbon it leaves. Compare the substitution of the old and new cation centres to decide whether rearrangement is stabilising.
Why not the others: (A) No ring is specified. (B) Charge remains positive. (D) A hydride shift does not cleave all C–C bonds.
Key point: Track both the migrating electron pair and the new charge site.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Propene reacts with HBr first without and then with peroxide, with the radical pathway effective in the second experiment. What major products are expected respectively?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2-bromopropane then 1-bromopropane.
Why: Ionic addition without peroxide proceeds through the more stable secondary carbocation, placing bromine on the middle carbon. The peroxide-initiated HBr radical chain favours the orientation that forms the more stable carbon radical and ultimately puts bromine on the terminal carbon. Peroxide supplies a radical chain pathway for HBr in the stated conditions; the Br radical adds so the more stable carbon radical forms before H abstraction. The ionic route instead optimises carbocation stability.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses the conditions. (B) Applies the radical result to both. (C) Omits the peroxide effect.
Key point: Choose the mechanism before choosing regioselectivity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: An optically active 2-bromobutane sample is divided. P undergoes clean backside SN2 substitution; Q is heated with a small alcoholic base and gives predominantly E2. Which combined outcome fits both mechanisms?
options: A) P inverts at C-2; Q mainly gives trans-but-2-ene among alkene isomers
B) P retains configuration; Q gives only but-1-ene
C) P racemises completely; Q gives only but-1-ene
D) P inverts; Q gives mainly butan-2-ol
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Inversion and a more substituted trans-favoured alkene.
Why: Backside displacement reverses the arrangement at the reacting stereocentre. E2 removes a β hydrogen with departure of bromide; with a small base, but-2-ene is generally favoured over but-1-ene, and its trans form is more stable than cis. These are separate stereochemical and regioselective decisions. An SN2 transition state requires backside approach and gives inversion at the stereocentre. E2 forms a double bond by removing a β proton and leaving group together, so the product lacks the same tetrahedral stereocentre.
Why not the others: (B) Gives retention and the less substituted alkene. (C) Assigns planar-intermediate racemisation to SN2. (D) Names a substitution alcohol rather than an E2 product.
Key point: Analyse each reaction condition independently.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Liquids X and Y each release gas with sodium metal. Only X gives the usual coloured complex with neutral FeCl₃. Which assignment is best supported?
options: B) X phenol; Y a simple aliphatic alcohol
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) X phenol, Y alcohol.
Why: Sodium reacts with acidic O–H groups in both alcohol and phenol, so that test alone does not distinguish them. A neutral ferric chloride colour is characteristic of the phenolic group in this qualitative comparison, selecting X as phenol. Neutral ferric chloride responds to phenolic oxygen through a coloured complex; sodium alone tests for sufficiently acidic O–H and is not selective. Combining both tests distinguishes phenol from a simple alcohol.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses the distinguishing observation. (C) Ether and alkane lack the O–H needed for the stated sodium response. (D) An alkane cannot explain X's tests.
Key point: Interpret the two tests together, not independently.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Ethanal is treated with dilute base at low temperature, then the isolated aldol product is warmed under dehydrating conditions. What is the pair of major carbon skeletons before and after dehydration?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3-hydroxybutanal then but-2-enal.
Why: Ethanal's enolate attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second ethanal, joining two C₂ units. Protonation yields CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₂–CHO, with the OH at the β carbon. Subsequent dehydration removes water across the α–β positions to give CH₃–CH=CH–CHO. The first low-temperature step creates a β-hydroxy aldehyde, not an α,β-unsaturated product. Warming removes water across the adjacent carbons, introducing the conjugated C=C while retaining the carbonyl group.
Why not the others: (A) Places OH at the wrong carbon and reduces rather than dehydrates. (B) Loses one carbon from the two ethanal units. (D) Places the carbonyl internally and loses oxygen entirely.
Key point: Count carbons and track the β-hydroxy carbonyl before eliminating water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: In water, aniline is appreciably less basic than cyclohexylamine. Which explanation addresses electron-pair availability at nitrogen?
options: A) Aniline has no nitrogen lone pair
C) The aniline nitrogen has a different valence
D) Aniline's lone pair delocalises into the benzene ring and is less available for protonation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Resonance lowers lone-pair availability.
Why: The aniline lone pair overlaps with the aromatic π system, stabilising the unprotonated base. Cyclohexylamine lacks this conjugation, so its lone pair is more available to accept a proton under comparable aqueous conditions. Solvation can matter, but the proposed resonance distinction is the central structural reason. Resonance donation of the aniline lone pair into the ring lowers its availability to bind a proton. The cyclohexylamine lone pair is localised on nitrogen and the alkyl framework does not delocalise it.
Why not the others: (A) The lone pair exists. (B) Cyclohexylamine is an amine. (C) Both nitrogens have ordinary amine valence.
Key point: Compare conjugation of the free base when assessing basicity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Osmotic pressure of mixed nonelectrolytes compared with an electrolyte
questions.question: At a fixed temperature, 0.020 mol glucose and 0.030 mol urea are dissolved to make 1.00 L of an ideal solution. Both are nonelectrolytes. What is its osmotic pressure divided by that of 0.020 M NaCl at the same temperature, if NaCl is taken as fully dissociated?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1.25.
Given: 0.020 mol glucose and 0.030 mol urea in 1.00 L; reference solution 0.020 M NaCl, fully dissociated.
Formula/Principle: \(\Pi=iCRT\), where \(iC\) is the total concentration of dissolved particles.
Step 1: Mixture: \(C=0.020+0.030=0.050\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}\) of particles (\(i=1\) for each).
Step 2: NaCl: \(i=2\), so particle concentration \(=2\times0.020=0.040\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}\).
Step 3: \(R\) and \(T\) cancel in the ratio.
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\Pi_{\text{mix}}}{\Pi_{\ce{NaCl}}}=\frac{0.050\,RT}{2(0.020)\,RT}=\frac{0.050}{0.040}=1.25\]
Why: Osmotic pressure is a colligative property: it depends on the number of dissolved particles, not on what they are. Glucose and urea stay as whole molecules, so their amounts simply add. Each NaCl unit gives two ions, so the reference solution has twice as many particles as its formula concentration suggests.
Why not the others: (B) 2.5 = 0.050/0.020 treats NaCl as if it did not dissociate. (C) 0.80 = 0.040/0.050 is the ratio upside down. (D) 0.625 = 0.050/0.080 applies the factor of two to NaCl twice.
Key point: Compare total particle concentrations, using i for electrolytes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Ag/Ag⁺ half-cells at 298 K contain 0.010 M and 1.0 M Ag⁺. With ideal solutions and negligible junction potential, use 0.059 V for 2.303RT/F. Which electrode is negative, and what emf results before appreciable composition change?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The dilute electrode; +0.118 V.
Given: \([\ce{Ag+}]=0.010\ \mathrm M\) and \(1.0\ \mathrm M\); \(2.303RT/F=0.059\ \mathrm V\); \(n=1\).
Formula/Principle: For \(\ce{Ag+ + e- -> Ag}\), \(E=E^\circ+0.059\log[\ce{Ag+}]\); \(E_{\text{cell}}=E_{\text{cathode}}-E_{\text{anode}}\).
Step 1: The electrode in 1.0 M solution has the higher reduction potential, so it is the cathode (positive).
Step 2: The electrode in 0.010 M solution is the anode (negative); silver is oxidised there.
Step 3: \(E_{\text{cell}}=0.059\log(1.0/0.010)=0.059\times2\).
Worked derivation: \[E_{\text{cell}}=\frac{0.059}{1}\log_{10}\frac{1.0}{0.010}=0.059\times2=0.118\ \mathrm V\]
Why: Both half-cells have the same standard potential, so the emf comes only from the concentration difference. The cell runs in the direction that evens out the concentrations: silver dissolves on the dilute side, raising its ion concentration, and silver ions plate out on the concentrated side. Electrons are released at the dilute electrode, which makes it the negative terminal.
Why not the others: (A) makes the concentrated electrode negative, but reduction, not oxidation, happens there. (C) 0.059 V counts one factor of ten; the concentrations differ by a factor of 100, which is two factors of ten. (D) reverses the polarity and gives a negative emf, which would describe a cell that does not run spontaneously.
Key point: In a concentration cell the dilute side is the anode and \(E=(0.059/n)\log(C_{\text{conc}}/C_{\text{dil}})\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The figure plots initial rates for trials 1–3 while one concentration is doubled at a time. Which empirical rate law follows?
questions.image_alt: Three trial bars show rate 2, 4 and 16 in units of 10^-3 M/s; concentration labels are trial 1 A=0.10,B=0.10 M; trial 2 A=0.20,B=0.10 M; trial 3 A=0.20,B=0.20 M.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) k[A][B]².
Given: Trial 1: [A] = 0.10 M, [B] = 0.10 M, rate 2 × 10⁻³ M/s. Trial 2: 0.20, 0.10, rate 4 × 10⁻³. Trial 3: 0.20, 0.20, rate 16 × 10⁻³.
Formula/Principle: For rate \(=k[A]^m[B]^n\), doubling one concentration alone multiplies the rate by \(2^m\) or \(2^n\).
Step 1: Trials 1 and 2: only [A] doubles; the rate ratio is \(4/2=2=2^m\), so \(m=1\).
Step 2: Trials 2 and 3: only [B] doubles; the rate ratio is \(16/4=4=2^n\), so \(n=2\).
Worked derivation: \[2^m=\frac{4}{2}=2\Rightarrow m=1;\qquad2^n=\frac{16}{4}=4\Rightarrow n=2;\qquad\text{rate}=k[A][B]^2\]
Why: Each pair of trials changes one concentration and holds the other fixed, so each rate ratio isolates one order. Orders come from experiment in this way and cannot be read from a balanced equation.
Why not the others: (A) \(k[A]^2[B]\) predicts the rate to quadruple from trial 1 to 2 and to double from 2 to 3, the reverse of what is seen. (B) \(k[A][B]\) predicts only a doubling from trial 2 to 3 (to 8), not 16. (D) \(k[A]^2[B]^2\) predicts trial 2 to be 8, not 4.
Key point: Compare trials in which only one concentration changes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Hess law with a reversed step and a change of amount
questions.question: On the same mole basis, ΔH(A→B)=+40 kJ/mol and ΔH(C→B)=+75 kJ/mol. What is the enthalpy change when 2 mol of C is converted completely into A?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) +70 kJ.
Given: \(\Delta H(A\to B)=+40\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\); \(\Delta H(C\to B)=+75\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\); 2 mol of C reacts.
Formula/Principle: Hess's law: enthalpy is a state function, so steps can be added. Reversing a step changes the sign of \(\Delta H\); the change scales with the amount.
Step 1: Target for one mole: \(C\to A\). Write it as \(C\to B\) followed by \(B\to A\).
Step 2: \(\Delta H(B\to A)=-40\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\) (reverse of the first step).
Step 3: \(\Delta H(C\to A)=+75+(-40)=+35\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).
Step 4: For 2 mol: \(2\times35=+70\ \mathrm{kJ}\).
Worked derivation: \[\Delta H(C\to A)=\Delta H(C\to B)-\Delta H(A\to B)=75-40=+35\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}};\qquad2\ \mathrm{mol}\times35=+70\ \mathrm{kJ}\]
Why: Both given reactions end at B, so B is the common point through which C can be linked to A. Going from C to B uses the second value as given; going from B back to A needs the first value with its sign reversed. Enthalpy is extensive, so two moles need twice the energy.
Why not the others: (A) −70 kJ is the value for the reverse change, 2A → 2C. (B) +230 kJ adds the two values without reversing the first step, then doubles: 2(40 + 75). (C) +35 kJ is correct for one mole of C but the question asks for two.
Key point: Draw the path through the common species, reverse signs where needed, then scale by the amount.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: 20.0 mL of 0.10 M HCl is titrated with 0.10 M NaOH. At 30.0 mL added, find pH at 25 °C, with additive volumes and Kw=10⁻¹⁴.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) pH 12.30.
Given: 20.0 mL of 0.10 M HCl; 30.0 mL of 0.10 M NaOH added; \(K_w=10^{-14}\).
Formula/Principle: Neutralise first (\(\ce{H+ + OH- -> H2O}\)), then use the excess reagent in the total volume. \(pH=14-pOH\).
Step 1: Acid \(=20.0\times0.10=2.0\ \mathrm{mmol}\); base \(=30.0\times0.10=3.0\ \mathrm{mmol}\).
Step 2: Excess \(\ce{OH-}=3.0-2.0=1.0\ \mathrm{mmol}\).
Step 3: Total volume \(=20.0+30.0=50.0\ \mathrm{mL}\).
Step 4: \([\ce{OH-}]=1.0/50.0=0.020\ \mathrm M\).
Worked derivation: \[pOH=-\log_{10}(0.020)=1.70;\qquad pH=14.00-1.70=12.30\]
Why: The equivalence point is at 20.0 mL, so at 30.0 mL the solution contains sodium chloride and leftover sodium hydroxide. NaCl does not affect the pH, so the excess strong base alone sets it, after allowing for dilution into the combined volume.
Why not the others: (B) 1.70 is the pOH, not the pH. (C) 7.00 is the pH at the equivalence point (20.0 mL), not beyond it. (D) 13.30 would need \([\ce{OH-}]=0.20\ \mathrm M\), ten times the actual excess concentration.
Key point: Moles first, then excess over total volume, then the logarithm.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A transition-metal ion has exactly one unpaired electron. Under the spin-only approximation, what magnetic moment in Bohr magnetons is predicted?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) √3 BM.
Given: Number of unpaired electrons \(n=1\).
Formula/Principle: Spin-only magnetic moment \(\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\) BM.
Step 1: Substitute \(n=1\).
Worked derivation: \[\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}=\sqrt{1\times3}=\sqrt3\approx1.73\ \mathrm{BM}\]
Why: In the spin-only model the moment depends only on the number of unpaired electrons; the orbital contribution is taken as quenched. Ions such as \(\ce{Ti^3+}\) (\(3d^1\)) and \(\ce{Cu^2+}\) (\(3d^9\)) have one unpaired electron and show moments close to 1.73 BM.
Why not the others: (A) 1 uses \(\sqrt{n}\) or just n, leaving out the factor \((n+2)\). (C) \(\sqrt8\) is the value for two unpaired electrons, \(\sqrt{2\times4}\). (D) 3 is \(n(n+2)\) without the square root.
Key point: \(\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\) BM: 1.73, 2.83, 3.87, 4.90, 5.92 for n = 1 to 5.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Distance from a centre to a tangent
questions.question: A circle with centre (3,4) touches the x-axis. Which ordinates occur where it intersects the positive y-axis?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4±√7.
Given: \(\text{centre }(3,4),\quad\text{tangent to }y=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(r=|y_c|,\quad(x-3)^2+(y-4)^2=r^2\)
Step 1: \(r=4\)
Step 2: \(x=0:\ 9+(y-4)^2=16\)
Step 3: \((y-4)^2=7\Rightarrow y=4\pm\sqrt7\)
Worked derivation: \[y_1=4+\sqrt7\approx6.65>0,\qquad y_2=4-\sqrt7\approx1.35>0\]
Check: \[|x_c|=3<r=4\Rightarrow\text{two intersections with }x=0\]
Why: \(d(\text{centre},\ x=0)=3<r\)
Why not the others: (A) \(4-\sqrt7>0\) omitted; (B) \(4+\sqrt7>0\) omitted; (D) \(3<4\Rightarrow(y-4)^2=7>0\).
Key point: \(x=0:\ (y-k)^2=r^2-h^2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: An ellipse centred at the origin has major axis along x, focus (3,0) and right directrix x=9. What are its eccentricity and full minor-axis length?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/√3 and 6√2.
Given: \(c=3,\quad\dfrac ae=9\)
Formula/Principle: \(c=ae,\quad b^2=a^2-c^2\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac ae\cdot ae=a^2=9\times3=27\)
Step 2: \(a=3\sqrt3,\quad e=\dfrac ca=\dfrac{3}{3\sqrt3}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\)
Step 3: \(b^2=27-9=18\Rightarrow b=3\sqrt2\)
Worked derivation: \[e=\frac{1}{\sqrt3},\qquad2b=2\times3\sqrt2=6\sqrt2\]
Check: \[\frac ae=\frac{3\sqrt3}{1/\sqrt3}=9,\qquad ae=3\sqrt3\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt3}=3\]
Why: \(\text{focus }(ae,0),\quad\text{directrix }x=\dfrac ae\)
Why not the others: (A) \(e=\tfrac13\Rightarrow a=9e=3,\ c=ae=1\neq3\); (C) \(b=3\sqrt2\neq2b\); (D) \(e=\sqrt3>1\).
Key point: \(a^2=c\cdot\dfrac ae\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For which real a is f(x)=x³−3ax²+3x strictly increasing for every real x?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) −1≤a≤1.
Given: \(f(x)=x^3-3ax^2+3x\)
Formula/Principle: \(f'(x)\ge0\ \forall x,\ \text{zeros isolated}\Rightarrow f\ \text{strictly increasing}\)
Step 1: \(f'(x)=3x^2-6ax+3=3\left[(x-a)^2+1-a^2\right]\)
Step 2: \(\min f'=3(1-a^2)\ \text{at }x=a\)
Step 3: \(3(1-a^2)\ge0\iff a^2\le1\)
Worked derivation: \[-1\le a\le1\]
Check: \[a=1:\ f'(x)=3(x-1)^2\ge0,\ f'=0\ \text{only at }x=1;\qquad a=-1:\ f'(x)=3(x+1)^2\]
Why: \(D=36a^2-36\le0\iff f'(x)\ge0\ \forall x\)
Why not the others: (A) \(a=\pm1:\ f'=3(x\mp1)^2\ge0\) excluded wrongly; (B) \(a=-2:\ f'(-2)=12-24+3=-9<0\); (D) \(a=2:\ f'(2)=12-24+3=-9<0\).
Key point: \(f'\ge0\ \text{with isolated zeros}\Rightarrow\text{strictly increasing}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Find the total area between y=x² and y=2−x² over −2≤x≤2.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 8.
Given: \(y_1=x^2,\quad y_2=2-x^2,\quad-2\le x\le2\)
Formula/Principle: \(A=\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}|y_2-y_1|\,dx\)
Step 1: \(x^2=2-x^2\Rightarrow x=\pm1\)
Step 2: \(A=2\left[\displaystyle\int_0^1(2-2x^2)\,dx+\int_1^2(2x^2-2)\,dx\right]\)
Step 3: \(\displaystyle\int_0^1(2-2x^2)\,dx=\left[2x-\tfrac23x^3\right]_0^1=\tfrac43\)
Step 4: \(\displaystyle\int_1^2(2x^2-2)\,dx=\left[\tfrac23x^3-2x\right]_1^2=\left(\tfrac{16}{3}-4\right)-\left(\tfrac23-2\right)=\tfrac83\)
Worked derivation: \[A=2\left(\frac43+\frac83\right)=2\times4=8\]
Check: \[\int_{-2}^{2}(2-2x^2)\,dx=8-\frac{32}{3}=-\frac83=2\left(\frac43-\frac83\right)\]
Why: \(|x|<1:\ y_2>y_1;\qquad1<|x|\le2:\ y_1>y_2\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\tfrac43+\tfrac83=4\) (\(\times2\) omitted); (C) \(2\times\tfrac83=\tfrac{16}{3}\) (\(|x|<1\) omitted); (D) \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}2x^2\,dx=\tfrac{32}{3}\).
Key point: \(A=\displaystyle\int|f-g|\,dx\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let f(x)=x²−4x+5 with domain x≥2. Which inverse value f⁻¹(10) is valid under that domain restriction?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 5.
Given: \(f(x)=x^2-4x+5,\quad x\ge2\)
Formula/Principle: \(f^{-1}(10)=x\iff f(x)=10,\ x\ge2\)
Step 1: \(f(x)=(x-2)^2+1\)
Step 2: \((x-2)^2+1=10\Rightarrow(x-2)^2=9\Rightarrow x=5\ \text{or}\ x=-1\)
Step 3: \(-1<2\Rightarrow\text{rejected}\)
Worked derivation: \[f^{-1}(u)=2+\sqrt{u-1},\qquad f^{-1}(10)=2+\sqrt9=5\]
Check: \[f(5)=25-20+5=10\]
Why: \(x\ge2\Rightarrow f\ \text{one-one}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(-1\notin[2,\infty)\); (B) \(-1\notin[2,\infty)\); (D) \(f(\sqrt{10})=15-4\sqrt{10}\approx2.35\neq10\).
Key point: \(f^{-1}(u)=2+\sqrt{u-1}\ \ (x\ge2)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For A with rows (1,2), (k,6), which k makes A singular?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3.
Given: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\k&6\end{pmatrix}\)
Formula/Principle: \(A\ \text{singular}\iff\det A=0\)
Step 1: \(\det A=1\cdot6-2\cdot k=6-2k\)
Step 2: \(6-2k=0\)
Worked derivation: \[k=3\]
Check: \[k=3:\ (3,6)=3\,(1,2)\]
Why: \(\det A=0\iff\text{rows proportional}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(k=2:\ \det A=2\neq0\); (B) \(k=6:\ \det A=-6\neq0\); (D) \(k=12:\ \det A=-18\neq0\).
Key point: \(\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}=ad-bc\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Factory A supplies 2/3 of parts with 1% defective; B supplies 1/3 with 4% defective. Given a defective part, what is the chance it came from B?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2/3.
Given: \(P(A)=\tfrac23,\ P(D|A)=0.01;\quad P(B)=\tfrac13,\ P(D|B)=0.04\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(B|D)=\dfrac{P(B)P(D|B)}{P(A)P(D|A)+P(B)P(D|B)}\)
Step 1: \(P(A)P(D|A)=\tfrac23\times0.01=\tfrac{0.02}{3}\)
Step 2: \(P(B)P(D|B)=\tfrac13\times0.04=\tfrac{0.04}{3}\)
Worked derivation: \[P(B|D)=\frac{0.04/3}{0.02/3+0.04/3}=\frac{0.04}{0.06}=\frac23\]
Check: \[P(A|D)=\frac{0.02}{0.06}=\frac13,\qquad\frac13+\frac23=1\]
Why: \(P(D)=P(A)P(D|A)+P(B)P(D|B)\)
Why not the others: (B) \(P(B)=\tfrac13\) (prior); (C) \(\tfrac12\) (\(P(A)P(D|A)=P(B)P(D|B)\) assumed); (D) \(\dfrac{0.04}{0.01+0.04}=\tfrac45\) (priors omitted).
Key point: \(P(B|D)\propto P(B)\,P(D|B)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Find the constant term in (x²−1/x)⁶ for x≠0.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 15.
Given: \(\left(x^2-\dfrac1x\right)^6,\quad x\ne0\)
Formula/Principle: \(T_{k}=\dbinom6k(x^2)^{6-k}\left(-\dfrac1x\right)^k\)
Step 1: \(T_k=\dbinom6k(-1)^kx^{12-2k-k}=\dbinom6k(-1)^kx^{12-3k}\)
Step 2: \(12-3k=0\Rightarrow k=4\)
Worked derivation: \[T_4=\binom64(-1)^4=15\]
Check: \[(x^2)^2\left(\frac1x\right)^4=x^4\cdot x^{-4}=x^0\]
Why: \(\text{constant term}\iff12-3k=0\)
Why not the others: (A) \((-1)^4=+1\neq-1\); (C) \(\dbinom63=20:\ k=3\Rightarrow x^{3}\); (D) \(-\dbinom63=-20:\ k=3\Rightarrow x^{3}\).
Key point: \(T_k=\dbinom nk a^{n-k}b^k\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Arithmetic progression from two partial sums
questions.question: An arithmetic progression has S₅=25 and S₁₀=100. What is its twentieth term?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 39.
Given: \(S_5=25,\quad S_{10}=100\)
Formula/Principle: \(S_n=\dfrac n2\left[2a+(n-1)d\right],\quad a_n=a+(n-1)d\)
Step 1: \(\tfrac52(2a+4d)=25\Rightarrow2a+4d=10\)
Step 2: \(5(2a+9d)=100\Rightarrow2a+9d=20\)
Step 3: \(5d=10\Rightarrow d=2,\quad a=1\)
Worked derivation: \[a_{20}=1+19\times2=39\]
Check: \[S_n=n^2:\ S_5=25,\ S_{10}=100,\quad a_{20}=S_{20}-S_{19}=400-361=39\]
Why: \(a=1,\ d=2\Rightarrow S_n=n^2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(a_{20}\ne20\) (\(a_n=2n-1\)); (B) \(a_{19}=37\); (C) \(a_{21}=41\).
Key point: \(a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Second-order radical limit from a first-order condition
questions.question: For real a, lim(x→0)[√(1+ax)−1]/x=3. Find lim(x→0)[√(1+ax)−1−3x]/x².
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) −9/2.
Given: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sqrt{1+ax}-1}{x}=3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sqrt p-q=\dfrac{p-q^2}{\sqrt p+q}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{\sqrt{1+ax}-1}{x}=\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{1+ax}+1}\to\dfrac a2=3\Rightarrow a=6\)
Step 2: \(\sqrt{1+6x}-(1+3x)=\dfrac{(1+6x)-(1+3x)^2}{\sqrt{1+6x}+1+3x}=\dfrac{-9x^2}{\sqrt{1+6x}+1+3x}\)
Worked derivation: \[\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sqrt{1+6x}-1-3x}{x^2}=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{-9}{\sqrt{1+6x}+1+3x}=\frac{-9}{2}\]
Check: \[\sqrt{1+t}=1+\frac t2-\frac{t^2}{8}+\dots,\quad t=6x:\ -\frac{36x^2}{8}=-\frac92x^2\]
Why: \((1+6x)-(1+3x)^2=-9x^2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(+\tfrac92\) (sign of \(-9x^2\) dropped); (B) \(-\dfrac{2a}{8}=-\tfrac32\) (\(a^2\to2a\)); (C) \(+\dfrac{2a}{8}=+\tfrac32\).
Key point: \(\sqrt{1+ax}=1+\dfrac a2x-\dfrac{a^2}{8}x^2+\dots\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: L₁: r=(1,0,0)+t(1,1,0); L₂: r=(0,0,2)+s(0,1,1). Find their shortest distance.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1/√3.
Given: \(\mathbf a_1=(1,0,0),\ \mathbf u=(1,1,0);\quad\mathbf a_2=(0,0,2),\ \mathbf v=(0,1,1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(d=\dfrac{|(\mathbf a_2-\mathbf a_1)\cdot(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)|}{|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|}\)
Step 1: \(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=(1\cdot1-0\cdot1,\ 0\cdot0-1\cdot1,\ 1\cdot1-1\cdot0)=(1,-1,1)\)
Step 2: \(|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|=\sqrt{1+1+1}=\sqrt3\)
Step 3: \(\mathbf a_2-\mathbf a_1=(-1,0,2)\)
Step 4: \((-1,0,2)\cdot(1,-1,1)=-1+0+2=1\)
Worked derivation: \[d=\frac{|1|}{\sqrt3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\]
Check: \[(1,-1,1)\cdot\mathbf u=1-1=0,\qquad(1,-1,1)\cdot\mathbf v=-1+1=0\]
Why: \(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\neq\mathbf 0,\quad(\mathbf a_2-\mathbf a_1)\cdot(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)\neq0\Rightarrow\text{skew}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(|(\mathbf a_2-\mathbf a_1)\cdot(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)|=1\) (\(\div\sqrt3\) omitted); (B) \(|z_2-z_1|=2\); (C) \(|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|=\sqrt3\).
Key point: \(d=\left|(\mathbf a_2-\mathbf a_1)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\right|,\quad\hat{\mathbf n}=\dfrac{\mathbf u\times\mathbf v}{|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Six distinct people A–F sit at a round table, rotations identical but reflections distinct. How many arrangements have A not beside B and C not beside D?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 48.
Given: \(6\ \text{people, circular};\quad X=\{A\ \text{beside}\ B\},\quad Y=\{C\ \text{beside}\ D\}\)
Formula/Principle: \(N=|U|-|X|-|Y|+|X\cap Y|,\quad|U|=(n-1)!\)
Step 1: \(|U|=5!=120\)
Step 2: \(|X|=|Y|=2\times(5-1)!=48\)
Step 3: \(|X\cap Y|=2\times2\times(4-1)!=24\)
Worked derivation: \[N=120-48-48+24=48\]
Check: \[|X\cup Y|=48+48-24=72,\qquad120-72=48\]
Why: \(|\overline X\cap\overline Y|=|U|-|X\cup Y|\)
Why not the others: (A) \(|X\cap Y|=24\); (C) \(120-48=72\) (\(Y\) ignored); (D) \(120-24=96\) (\(|X\cap Y|\) only).
Key point: \(|\overline X\cap\overline Y|=|U|-|X|-|Y|+|X\cap Y|\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Modulus and conjugate: condition for a real value
questions.question: A non-real complex number z satisfies the condition that z + 4/z is a real number. What is |z|?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2.
Given: \(z=x+iy,\quad y\ne0,\quad z+\dfrac4z\in\mathbb R\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1z=\dfrac{\bar z}{|z|^2}\)
Step 1: \(z+\dfrac4z=x+iy+\dfrac{4(x-iy)}{x^2+y^2}\)
Step 2: \(\operatorname{Im}\left(z+\dfrac4z\right)=y-\dfrac{4y}{x^2+y^2}=y\left(1-\dfrac{4}{x^2+y^2}\right)\)
Step 3: \(y\ne0\Rightarrow1-\dfrac{4}{x^2+y^2}=0\)
Worked derivation: \[x^2+y^2=4\Rightarrow|z|=2\]
Check: \[z=2i:\ 2i+\frac{4}{2i}=2i-2i=0\in\mathbb R\]
Why: \(w\in\mathbb R\iff\operatorname{Im}w=0\)
Why not the others: (B) \(z=4i:\ 4i+\dfrac{4}{4i}=4i-i=3i\notin\mathbb R\); (C) \(z=\tfrac i2:\ \tfrac i2+\dfrac{4}{i/2}=\tfrac i2-8i\notin\mathbb R\); (D) \(z=\sqrt2\,i:\ \sqrt2\,i-2\sqrt2\,i\notin\mathbb R\).
Key point: \(z+\dfrac kz\in\mathbb R,\ z\notin\mathbb R\Rightarrow|z|^2=k\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: First-order linear equation with initial value
questions.question: Solve y′+2y=e^(−x), y(0)=0. What is y(ln 2)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/4.
Given: \(y'+2y=e^{-x},\quad y(0)=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{I.F.}=e^{\int2\,dx}=e^{2x},\quad\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{2x}y\right)=e^{2x}e^{-x}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{2x}y\right)=e^{x}\)
Step 2: \(e^{2x}y=e^x+C\)
Step 3: \(y(0)=0:\ 0=1+C\Rightarrow C=-1\)
Step 4: \(y=e^{-x}-e^{-2x}\)
Worked derivation: \[y(\ln2)=e^{-\ln2}-e^{-2\ln2}=\frac12-\frac14=\frac14\]
Check: \[y'+2y=\left(-e^{-x}+2e^{-2x}\right)+2\left(e^{-x}-e^{-2x}\right)=e^{-x}\]
Why: \(y'+Py=Q\Rightarrow y\,e^{\int P\,dx}=\displaystyle\int Q\,e^{\int P\,dx}\,dx+C\)
Why not the others: (A) \(e^{-\ln2}=\tfrac12\) (\(C=0\)); (C) \(\tfrac12+\tfrac14=\tfrac34\) (\(C=+1\)); (D) \(e^{0}=1\).
Key point: \(y=e^{-x}-e^{-2x}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: How many distinct solutions of sin(2x)=cos x lie in 0≤x<2π?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4.
Given: \(\sin2x=\cos x,\quad0\le x<2\pi\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x\)
Step 1: \(2\sin x\cos x-\cos x=0\Rightarrow\cos x\,(2\sin x-1)=0\)
Step 2: \(\cos x=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac\pi2,\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\)
Step 3: \(\sin x=\dfrac12\Rightarrow x=\dfrac\pi6,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\)
Worked derivation: \[x\in\left\{\frac\pi6,\ \frac\pi2,\ \frac{5\pi}{6},\ \frac{3\pi}{2}\right\}\Rightarrow4\]
Check: \[x=\frac{3\pi}{2}:\ \sin3\pi=0=\cos\frac{3\pi}{2};\qquad x=\frac{5\pi}{6}:\ \sin\frac{5\pi}{3}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}\]
Why: \(ab=0\iff a=0\ \text{or}\ b=0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(2\) (\(\cos x=0\) roots lost by division); (B) \(3\ne4\) (\(x=\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\) omitted); (C) \(5\ne4\) (\(x=2\pi\notin[0,2\pi)\)).
Key point: \(\cos x\,(2\sin x-1)=0\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Masses 3m and m hang over a light frictionless pulley fixed to a lift accelerating upward at g. Relative to the lift, what is the magnitude of their acceleration?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) g.
Given: \(m_1=3m,\quad m_2=m,\quad a_{\text{lift}}=g\ \text{(upward)}\)
Formula/Principle: \(g_{\text{eff}}=g+a_{\text{lift}};\quad\text{lift frame: }m_1g_{\text{eff}}-T=m_1a,\quad T-m_2g_{\text{eff}}=m_2a\)
Step 1: \(g_{\text{eff}}=g+g=2g\)
Step 2: \((m_1-m_2)\,g_{\text{eff}}=(m_1+m_2)\,a\)
Step 3: \(a=\dfrac{3m-m}{3m+m}\,g_{\text{eff}}=\dfrac12\,g_{\text{eff}}\)
Worked derivation: \[a=\frac12(2g)=g\]
Check: \[T=m_2(g_{\text{eff}}+a)=m(2g+g)=3mg;\qquad3m(2g)-3mg=3m\,a\Rightarrow a=g\]
Why: \(\text{pseudo-force }=-m\,\mathbf a_{\text{lift}}\Rightarrow g_{\text{eff}}=g+a_{\text{lift}}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\tfrac12g\) (\(g_{\text{eff}}=g\)); (C) \(2g=g_{\text{eff}}\) (\(\times\tfrac12\) omitted); (D) \(m_1\ne m_2\Rightarrow a\ne0\).
Key point: \(a_{\text{rel}}=\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{m_1+m_2}\,(g+a_{\text{lift}})\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Work by a position-dependent force and the work–energy theorem
questions.question: A block of mass 2 kg starts from rest at x=0 on a frictionless horizontal surface. The only horizontal force on it acts along +x and has magnitude F(x)=2x N, with x in metres. What is the speed of the block at x=3 m?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3 m/s.
Given: \(m=2\ \mathrm{kg},\quad u=0,\quad F(x)=2x\ \mathrm N,\quad x:0\to3\ \mathrm m\)
Formula/Principle: \(W=\displaystyle\int F\,dx,\quad W=\tfrac12mv^2-\tfrac12mu^2\)
Step 1: \(W=\displaystyle\int_0^3 2x\,dx=\left[x^2\right]_0^3=9\ \mathrm J\)
Step 2: \(\tfrac12(2)v^2-0=9\)
Step 3: \(v^2=9\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}\)
Worked derivation: \[v=\sqrt{\frac{2W}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\times9}{2}}=3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\]
Check: \[W=\tfrac12\times3\ \mathrm m\times6\ \mathrm N=9\ \mathrm J\quad(\text{area under }F\text{–}x)\]
Why: \(F=F(x)\Rightarrow W=\displaystyle\int F\,dx\neq F\,\Delta x\)
Why not the others: (A) \(W=F(3)\times3=18\ \mathrm J\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{18}=3\sqrt2\); (B) \(\dfrac Wm=4.5\) (not a speed); (C) \(v=W=9\) (\(\tfrac12mv^2\) not used).
Key point: \(\tfrac12mv^2=\displaystyle\int_0^xF\,dx'\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Escape speed versus distance from centre
questions.question: Neglecting atmosphere and rotation, a planet's escape speed is v at radius R from its centre. What is escape speed at radius 4R?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) v/2.
Given: \(v_{\text{esc}}(R)=v\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tfrac12mv_{\text{esc}}^2-\dfrac{GMm}{r}=0\Rightarrow v_{\text{esc}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{r}}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{v_{\text{esc}}(4R)}{v_{\text{esc}}(R)}=\sqrt{\dfrac{R}{4R}}\)
Worked derivation: \[v_{\text{esc}}(4R)=v\sqrt{\frac14}=\frac v2\]
Check: \[\tfrac12m\left(\tfrac v2\right)^2=\tfrac14\left(\tfrac12mv^2\right)=\tfrac14\cdot\frac{GMm}{R}=\frac{GMm}{4R}\]
Why: \(E_{\text{total}}=0\ \text{at escape}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac v4\) (\(v\propto r^{-1}\)); (B) \(4v\) (\(v\propto r\)); (D) \(2v\) (\(v\propto\sqrt r\)).
Key point: \(v_{\text{esc}}\propto r^{-1/2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A reversibly loaded material follows a straight stress–strain line from (0,0) to (2ε,2S), where ε and S are positive. What energy density is stored at strain 2ε?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2Sε.
Given: \(\sigma=\dfrac{S}{\varepsilon}\,\varepsilon',\quad0\le\varepsilon'\le2\varepsilon\)
Formula/Principle: \(u=\displaystyle\int_0^{\varepsilon_f}\sigma\,d\varepsilon'\)
Step 1: \(u=\displaystyle\int_0^{2\varepsilon}\frac{S}{\varepsilon}\,\varepsilon'\,d\varepsilon'=\frac{S}{\varepsilon}\cdot\frac{(2\varepsilon)^2}{2}\)
Worked derivation: \[u=\frac12(2\varepsilon)(2S)=2S\varepsilon\]
Check: \[[u]=[\sigma][\varepsilon]=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\]
Why: \(u=\tfrac12\,\sigma_f\,\varepsilon_f\ \ (\text{linear})\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac12(\varepsilon)(2S)=S\varepsilon\) (\(\varepsilon_f=\varepsilon\)); (C) \(\tfrac12(2\varepsilon)(2S)+\tfrac12(\varepsilon)(2S)=3S\varepsilon\) (extra triangle added); (D) \((2\varepsilon)(2S)=4S\varepsilon\) (\(\tfrac12\) omitted).
Key point: \(u=\tfrac12\times\text{stress}\times\text{strain}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Ice-water calorimetry with a phase change
questions.question: An insulated vessel mixes 100 g ice at 0 °C with 300 g water at 50 °C. Use cwater=4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and Lfusion=336 J g⁻¹. Neglect vessel heat capacity. Find final temperature.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 17.5 °C.
Given: \(m_i=100\ \mathrm g\ (0^\circ\mathrm C),\quad m_w=300\ \mathrm g\ (50^\circ\mathrm C),\quad c=4.2\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}K^{-1}},\quad L=336\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(Q_{\text{lost}}=Q_{\text{gained}},\quad Q=mc\,\Delta T,\quad Q=mL\)
Step 1: \(Q_{\text{max}}=300\times4.2\times50=63000\ \mathrm J\)
Step 2: \(Q_{\text{melt}}=100\times336=33600\ \mathrm J<63000\ \mathrm J\)
Step 3: \(300(4.2)(50-T)=33600+100(4.2)(T-0)\)
Step 4: \(63000-1260T=33600+420T\Rightarrow1680T=29400\)
Worked derivation: \[T=\frac{29400}{1680}=17.5^\circ\mathrm C\]
Check: \[Q_{\text{lost}}=300(4.2)(32.5)=40950\ \mathrm J;\qquad Q_{\text{gained}}=33600+100(4.2)(17.5)=40950\ \mathrm J\]
Why: \(Q_{\text{max}}>Q_{\text{melt}}\Rightarrow\text{all ice melts},\ T>0^\circ\mathrm C\)
Why not the others: (B) \(63000\ \mathrm J>33600\ \mathrm J\); (C) \(T=25:\ 300(4.2)(25)=31500\ \mathrm J\ne33600+10500=44100\ \mathrm J\); (D) \(T=31.5:\ 300(4.2)(18.5)=23310\ \mathrm J\ne33600+13230=46830\ \mathrm J\).
Key point: \(m_wc(T_w-T)=m_iL+m_ic(T-0)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: RMS-speed ratio at different temperatures and molar masses
questions.question: Two ideal gases have molar masses in the ratio 4:9. The first is at absolute temperature T and the second is at 4T. What is the ratio of their rms speeds, in the same order?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3:4.
Given: \(M_1:M_2=4:9,\quad T_1=T,\quad T_2=4T\)
Formula/Principle: \(v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{v_1^2}{v_2^2}=\dfrac{T_1/M_1}{T_2/M_2}=\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}\cdot\dfrac{M_2}{M_1}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{v_1^2}{v_2^2}=\dfrac14\times\dfrac94=\dfrac{9}{16}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{v_1}{v_2}=\sqrt{\frac{9}{16}}=\frac34\]
Check: \[M_1=4,\ T_1=1:\ v_1\propto\sqrt{\tfrac14}=0.50;\qquad M_2=9,\ T_2=4:\ v_2\propto\sqrt{\tfrac49}=0.667;\qquad\frac{0.50}{0.667}=0.75\]
Why: \(\tfrac12M v_{\text{rms}}^2=\tfrac32RT\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{M_1}{M_2}=\dfrac49\); (B) \(\sqrt{\dfrac{M_2}{M_1}}=\dfrac32\) (\(T_1=T_2\)); (C) \(\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}=\dfrac43\).
Key point: \(v_{\text{rms}}\propto\sqrt{T/M}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Period of series and parallel springs
questions.question: Two identical springs of constant k support the same mass m, first in series and then in parallel. What is Tseries/Tparallel for small oscillations?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2.
Given: \(k_1=k_2=k,\quad m\)
Formula/Principle: \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k_{\text{eff}}}};\quad\dfrac{1}{k_s}=\dfrac1k+\dfrac1k;\quad k_p=k+k\)
Step 1: \(k_s=\dfrac k2\)
Step 2: \(k_p=2k\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{T_s}{T_p}=\sqrt{\dfrac{k_p}{k_s}}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{T_s}{T_p}=\sqrt{\frac{2k}{k/2}}=\sqrt4=2\]
Check: \[T_s=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2m}{k}},\qquad T_p=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{2k}},\qquad\frac{T_s}{T_p}=\sqrt{2\times2}=2\]
Why: \(\text{series: equal force, extensions add};\quad\text{parallel: equal extension, forces add}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{T_p}{T_s}=\dfrac12\); (B) \(\sqrt2\) (\(k_s=k\) or \(k_p=k\)); (D) \(\dfrac{k_p}{k_s}=4\) (square root omitted).
Key point: \(T\propto k_{\text{eff}}^{-1/2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Energy of disconnected series capacitors after dielectric insertion
questions.question: Capacitors C and 2C are in series with charge Q after disconnection from a source. A dielectric doubles only the first capacitance with no leakage. Find final/initial ratios of total stored energy and voltage on the modified element.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2/3 and 1/2.
Given: \(C_1=C\to2C,\quad C_2=2C,\quad Q=\text{const}\)
Formula/Principle: \(U=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C},\quad V=\dfrac QC\)
Step 1: \(U_i=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}+\dfrac{Q^2}{2(2C)}=\dfrac{3Q^2}{4C}\)
Step 2: \(U_f=\dfrac{Q^2}{2(2C)}+\dfrac{Q^2}{2(2C)}=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}\)
Step 3: \(V_{1,i}=\dfrac QC,\quad V_{1,f}=\dfrac{Q}{2C}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{U_f}{U_i}=\frac{Q^2/2C}{3Q^2/4C}=\frac23,\qquad\frac{V_{1,f}}{V_{1,i}}=\frac{Q/2C}{Q/C}=\frac12\]
Check: \[U_f<U_i\quad(\text{dielectric pulled in});\qquad V_{2}=\frac{Q}{2C}\ \text{unchanged}\]
Why: \(\text{disconnected}\Rightarrow Q\ \text{constant on each plate}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{U_i}{U_f}=\dfrac32\); (C) \(\dfrac{V_{1,i}}{V_{1,f}}=2\); (D) \(U_f=\tfrac23U_i\ne U_i\).
Key point: \(Q=\text{const}\Rightarrow U\propto\dfrac1C,\ V\propto\dfrac1C\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Magnetic force with two field components
questions.question: A positive charge q moves at speed v along +x in field B(ĵ+k̂), with B>0. Which magnetic-force vector acts on it?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) qvB(k̂−ĵ).
Given: \(\mathbf v=v\,\hat{\mathbf i},\quad\mathbf B=B(\hat{\mathbf j}+\hat{\mathbf k}),\quad q>0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\mathbf F=q\,\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\)
Step 1: \(\hat{\mathbf i}\times\hat{\mathbf j}=\hat{\mathbf k}\)
Step 2: \(\hat{\mathbf i}\times\hat{\mathbf k}=-\hat{\mathbf j}\)
Worked derivation: \[\mathbf F=qvB\left(\hat{\mathbf i}\times\hat{\mathbf j}+\hat{\mathbf i}\times\hat{\mathbf k}\right)=qvB(\hat{\mathbf k}-\hat{\mathbf j})\]
Check: \[\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=0,\qquad\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf B=qvB^2(-1+1)=0\]
Why: \(\mathbf F\perp\mathbf v,\quad\mathbf F\perp\mathbf B\)
Why not the others: (B) \(q\,\mathbf B\times\mathbf v=qvB(\hat{\mathbf j}-\hat{\mathbf k})\) (order reversed); (C) \(\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf B=2qvB^2\ne0\); (D) \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\ne\mathbf 0\) (\(\mathbf v\nparallel\mathbf B\)).
Key point: \(|\mathbf F|=qvB\sqrt2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Potential change from a signed field graph
questions.question: The figure shows Eₓ as a function of x between 0 and 3a, with E₀,a>0. What is V(3a)−V(0)?
questions.image_alt: E_x is +2E0 from x=0 to a and −E0 from x=a to 3a, with horizontal constant segments and labelled axes.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Zero.
Given: \(E_x=+2E_0\ (0<x<a),\quad E_x=-E_0\ (a<x<3a)\)
Formula/Principle: \(V(x_2)-V(x_1)=-\displaystyle\int_{x_1}^{x_2}E_x\,dx\)
Step 1: \(\displaystyle\int_0^aE_x\,dx=2E_0a\)
Step 2: \(\displaystyle\int_a^{3a}E_x\,dx=-E_0(2a)=-2E_0a\)
Worked derivation: \[V(3a)-V(0)=-\left(2E_0a-2E_0a\right)=0\]
Check: \[V(a)-V(0)=-2E_0a,\qquad V(3a)-V(a)=+2E_0a\]
Why: \(E_x=-\dfrac{dV}{dx}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(-(2E_0a+2E_0a)=-4E_0a\) (\(|E_x|\) used); (B) \(-2E_0a=V(a)-V(0)\); (C) \(+2E_0a=V(3a)-V(a)\).
Key point: \(\Delta V=-(\text{signed area under }E_x\text{–}x)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Balanced Wheatstone bridge and the current drawn at balance
questions.question: A Wheatstone bridge has upper and lower left arms of 2 Ω and 3 Ω, and upper and lower right arms of 4 Ω and R. An ideal galvanometer joins the two midpoints and shows zero current. An ideal 10 V battery is connected between the top and bottom junctions. What are R and the current drawn from the battery?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 6 Ω and 3 A.
Given: \(P=2\ \Omega,\ Q=3\ \Omega\ (\text{left});\quad4\ \Omega,\ R\ (\text{right});\quad I_g=0;\quad V=10\ \mathrm V\)
Formula/Principle: \(I_g=0\iff\dfrac{2}{3}=\dfrac{4}{R};\quad I=\dfrac{V}{R_{\text{eq}}}\)
Step 1: \(2R=12\Rightarrow R=6\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(R_{\text{left}}=2+3=5\ \Omega,\quad R_{\text{right}}=4+6=10\ \Omega\)
Step 3: \(I_{\text{left}}=\dfrac{10}{5}=2\ \mathrm A,\quad I_{\text{right}}=\dfrac{10}{10}=1\ \mathrm A\)
Worked derivation: \[I=I_{\text{left}}+I_{\text{right}}=2+1=3\ \mathrm A\]
Check: \[V_{\text{mid,left}}=10-2(2)=6\ \mathrm V,\qquad V_{\text{mid,right}}=10-1(4)=6\ \mathrm V\]
Why: \(I_g=0\Rightarrow\text{two independent series branches}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(I_{\text{left}}=2\ \mathrm A\) only; (B) \(2\times3=4R\Rightarrow R=1.5\ \Omega\) (wrong arm pairing); (D) \(I_{\text{right}}=1\ \mathrm A\) only.
Key point: \(\dfrac PQ=\dfrac{R_3}{R_4}\Rightarrow I_g=0\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Lens and plane mirror on a common axis
questions.question: The figure places an object 30 cm left of a converging lens of focal length 10 cm and a plane mirror 20 cm right of the lens. After reflection and a second lens passage, where is the final image? Use paraxial rays.
options: A) 15 cm left of the lens
B) 50/3 cm left of the lens
C) 25 cm right of the lens
D) 50/3 cm right of the lens
questions.image_alt: Object O lies 30 cm left of a converging lens marked f=10 cm; a plane mirror is 20 cm right of the lens, perpendicular to the optical axis. No image positions are drawn.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 50/3 cm left.
Given: \(u_1=30\ \mathrm{cm},\quad f=10\ \mathrm{cm},\quad\text{mirror }20\ \mathrm{cm}\ \text{right of lens}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1f=\dfrac1u+\dfrac1v\ (\text{real distances});\quad\text{plane mirror: image distance}=\text{object distance}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{v_1}=\dfrac1{10}-\dfrac1{30}=\dfrac{2}{30}\Rightarrow v_1=15\ \mathrm{cm}\ (\text{right})\)
Step 2: \(\text{distance from mirror}=20-15=5\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 3: \(\text{mirror image at }20+5=25\ \mathrm{cm}\ \text{right of lens}\Rightarrow u_2=25\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 4: \(\dfrac{1}{v_2}=\dfrac1{10}-\dfrac1{25}=\dfrac{3}{50}\)
Worked derivation: \[v_2=\frac{50}{3}\ \mathrm{cm}\ (\text{left of lens})\]
Check: \[\frac{3}{50}+\frac{1}{25}=\frac{5}{50}=\frac{1}{10}\]
Why: \(\text{light returns leftward}\Rightarrow\text{final image on the left}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(v_1=15\ \mathrm{cm}\) (first image, on the right); (C) \(25\ \mathrm{cm}\) right (mirror image, \(u_2\)); (D) \(\tfrac{50}{3}\ \mathrm{cm}\) right (side of returning light reversed).
Key point: \(\text{image of one element}=\text{object of the next}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.sub_topic: Threshold frequency from two stopping potentials
questions.question: Stopping potentials for light frequencies f and 2f are 1 V and 3 V for one metal. What is its threshold frequency in terms of f?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) f/2.
Given: \(V_1=1\ \mathrm V\ (f),\quad V_2=3\ \mathrm V\ (2f)\)
Formula/Principle: \(eV_s=h\nu-\phi,\quad\phi=hf_0\)
Step 1: \(e(1\ \mathrm V)=hf-\phi\)
Step 2: \(e(3\ \mathrm V)=2hf-\phi\)
Step 3: \(e(2\ \mathrm V)=hf\)
Step 4: \(\phi=hf-e(1\ \mathrm V)=2\ \mathrm{eV}-1\ \mathrm{eV}=1\ \mathrm{eV}=\dfrac{hf}{2}\)
Worked derivation: \[f_0=\frac{\phi}{h}=\frac{hf/2}{h}=\frac f2\]
Check: \[2hf-\phi=4\ \mathrm{eV}-1\ \mathrm{eV}=3\ \mathrm{eV}\]
Why: \(K_{\max}=eV_s\)
Why not the others: (B) \(f_0=\tfrac f3\Rightarrow eV_1=\tfrac23hf=\tfrac43\ \mathrm{eV}\ne1\ \mathrm{eV}\); (C) \(f_0=f\Rightarrow V_1=0\); (D) \(f_0=2f\Rightarrow V_2=0\).
Key point: \(h=\dfrac{e\,\Delta V_s}{\Delta\nu}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: In hydrogen, what is wavelength ratio λ(3→2)/λ(2→1) for emitted photons? Use Eₙ=−13.6/n² eV.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 27/5.
Given: \(E_n=-\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\)
Step 1: \(\Delta E_{32}=13.6\left(\dfrac14-\dfrac19\right)=13.6\times\dfrac{5}{36}\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Step 2: \(\Delta E_{21}=13.6\left(1-\dfrac14\right)=13.6\times\dfrac34\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{\lambda_{32}}{\lambda_{21}}=\dfrac{\Delta E_{21}}{\Delta E_{32}}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\lambda_{32}}{\lambda_{21}}=\frac{3/4}{5/36}=\frac34\times\frac{36}{5}=\frac{27}{5}\]
Check: \[\lambda_{32}\approx656\ \mathrm{nm},\quad\lambda_{21}\approx122\ \mathrm{nm},\quad\frac{656}{122}\approx5.4\]
Why: \(\lambda\propto\dfrac{1}{\Delta E}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{\Delta E_{32}}{\Delta E_{21}}=\dfrac{5}{27}\) (inverted); (B) \(\dfrac{1/5}{1/9}=\dfrac95\) (\(n_1^2n_2^2\) factors dropped); (C) \(\dfrac59\) (inverse of that).
Key point: \(\dfrac1\lambda=R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2}-\dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A loop lies in the page. Magnetic flux into the page increases. Viewed facing the page, what is the induced conventional current direction?
options: D) No current because field direction is unchanged
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Counterclockwise, producing outward field.
Given: \(\Phi_{\text{in}}\ \text{increasing}:\ \dfrac{d\Phi_{\text{in}}}{dt}>0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\mathcal E=-\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{d\Phi_{\text{in}}}{dt}>0\Rightarrow\mathbf B_{\text{induced}}\ \text{out of the page}\)
Step 2: \(\mathbf B_{\text{induced}}\ \text{out of the page}\Rightarrow I\ \text{counterclockwise (right-hand rule)}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{d\Phi_{\text{in}}}{dt}>0\ \Rightarrow\ \mathbf B_{\text{induced}}=\odot\ \Rightarrow\ I=\circlearrowleft\]
Check: \[\Phi_{\text{induced}}\cdot\Delta\Phi_{\text{applied}}<0\]
Why: \(\mathcal E=-\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}\ \ (\text{Lenz})\)
Why not the others: (A) \(I=\circlearrowright\Rightarrow\mathbf B_{\text{induced}}=\otimes\Rightarrow\Phi_{\text{in}}\ \text{reinforced}\); (B) \(I=\circlearrowright\Rightarrow\mathbf B_{\text{induced}}=\otimes\ne\odot\); (D) \(\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}\ne0\Rightarrow\mathcal E\ne0\).
Key point: \(\mathbf B_{\text{induced}}\ \text{opposes}\ \Delta\Phi,\ \text{not}\ \Phi\)
